newsitem.title: UK: Adams urges British concessions for IRA truce.
newsitem.headline: Adams urges British concessions for IRA truce.

text.p: Gerry Adams, head of the IRA's political wing, said on Saturday he will press for a guerrilla ceasefire if Britain makes key concessions to bring his party into peace talks.
Adams, under mounting pressure by political opponents to urge an unconditional end to escalating violence in British-ruled Northern Ireland, insisted hopes still flickered for a lasting peace.

"When a meaningful and inclusive process of negotiations is genuinely being offered we could, with credibility, seek to persuade the IRA to restore the cessation (of violence) of August 1994. In our view that is the only effective way to proceeed," the Sinn Fein leader wrote in the Irish Times newspaper.
"It remains my firm view that an opportunity to rebuild the peace process and secure a permanent peace still exists," he asserted.

The Dublin paper said Adams's article contained views he had aired previously but that it might be a "coded signal" to London that Sinn Fein and the Irish Republican Army wanted to try to bridge a gulf blighting peace efforts for more than a year.
His comments come at a time of gloom over prospects for political progress in the troubled province.
Politicians fear further IRA violence and a repeat of last summer's sectarian conflict when the province was in turmoil during contentious parades by pro-British Protestants.

David Trimble, leader of the mainstream Ulster Unionist Party, was quoted on Saturday as saying that Protestants should be allowed to march in the Garvaghy Road area of Portadown in July. A march there last July lit the fuse of widepread trouble.
"Garvaghy Road is the main thoroughfare. There is a duty on the authorities to make sure that the Queen's highway is available to all..," Trimble told The Irish-American Post magazine.

An Anglo-Irish sponsored peace initiative was shattered by fresh IRA violence last year. A truce by pro-British Loyalist guerrillas is unstable. Multi-party talks from which Sinn Fein is excluded have made little headway.
Calling on Britain to remove what he termed its "veto" on Sinn Fein's entry into all-party peace talks, Adams declared that any new IRA truce would be "genuinely unequivocal".

Britain says an IRA truce that collapsed last year was phoney. It says the IRA, fighting a 28 year war to end rule from London, used it to lay plans for a campaign that has seen a lethal bombing wave in British cities and the re-emergence of bomb and gun ambushes on security forces in Northern Ireland.
Prime Minister John Major says Sinn Fein will be admitted to the talks only after his intelligence agencies are satisfied that any future IRA truce is meant to last.
Adams urged Major, who has spurned similar Sinn Fein offers of a truce linked to talks, not to allow the impending British general election to slow a peace momentum.

"I firmly believe that if clear assurances are given by the British government that a negotiations process which is both viable and credible will be put in place then the peace process can be restored..," he wrote.

He set out a series of demands in support of his party's long-standing insistence on speedy entry to talks. Demands for a guerrilla arms surrender must not be allowed to block talks negotiations, he said.
"Sinn Fein believes that an unequivocal restoration of the IRA cessation would represent the most important confidence-building initiative on the IRA's part.

"For its part, and as part of an inititive to rebuild the peace process the British government should outline...the substance of a programmatic approach on issues which will generate confidence..." Adams said.

Last Thursday, John Hume, leader of the moderate nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party, rejected Sinn Fein suggestions of a pact in the general election that must be called by May 22. He challenged Sinn Fein to call on the IRA to abandon its war immediately.
